uncited: Octree-based structures organize sparse volumetric data into a hierarchical tree where each node has eight children, enabling efficient storage and traversal of large datasets with significant empty space.

This family differs from sibling tree-based structures by its fixed 8-way branching factor and specific implementation strategies for memory layout (implicit vs. explicit) and topology (shallow fixed-depth vs. deep variable-depth).

Unlike [Sparse Voxel DAGs](2791-sparse-voxel-dags.md) which merge identical nodes to save space, or [Compact pointer trees](844-compact-pointer-tree.md) which use pointer compression, octrees typically rely on Morton ordering or fixed bit-masks for navigation.
All octree-based structures share the fundamental property of recursive spatial subdivision.
The 3D domain is divided into a bounding box, which is recursively split into eight octants until a stopping criterion (such as uniform data density or maximum depth) is met.
**Morton Ordering (Z-order curve):** Many implementations, particularly implicit ones, map 3D coordinates $(x, y, z)$ to a 1D integer key using Morton codes.
This preserves spatial locality, allowing linear arrays to represent tree structures and enabling efficient neighbor lookups and range queries.

**Sparsity Handling:** Empty or uniform regions are represented by a single node (or null pointer in implicit structures) rather than storing individual voxel values, providing compression ratios proportional to the sparsity of the data.
**Traversal:** Accessing data requires traversing from the root to the leaf.
The complexity is $O(\log N)$ for deep trees or $O(1)$ for shallow trees with direct indexing, where $N$ is the resolution.
The concept of octrees for volume representation dates back to the early days of 3D computer graphics, with foundational work by Meagher (1982) and others.
